claim: Let a party system be represented by a nonincreasing positive-integer profile \(x_1\ge\cdots\ge x_k>0\) with common total \(N=\sum_i x_i\), and compare only two profiles having the same \(N\), the same actual party count \(k\), and the same leading-party count \(x_1\). For shares \(p_i=x_i/N\), let the Laakso–Taagepera effective number be \(N_{LT}=1/\sum_i p_i^2\) and the Golosov effective number be \(N_G=\sum_i p_i/(p_i+p_1^2-p_i^2)\). The two indices induce the same weak ordering on every such comparison for \(N\le9\). At \(N=10\), strict reversal appears for the first time, and the complete first layer consists of the single unordered pair \((4,4,2)\) versus \((4,3,3)\). Laakso–Taagepera ranks \((4,3,3)\) as more fragmented because \(25/9<50/17\), whereas Golosov ranks \((4,4,2)\) as more fragmented because \(21/8>97/37\), with exact Golosov gap \(1/296\). Thus, even after fixing both the number of parties and the leading-party share at \(2/5\), redistributing one unit from the second party to the third can reverse the two effective-party rankings. Common positive scaling preserves both indices, so this strict reversal recurs at every total \(10q\) for positive integer \(q\).
integrity: Both indices are evaluated as exact rational functions of the integer profile. Two independent partition generators agree on every profile through the sharp total, and exhaustive same-\((k,x_1)\) comparison proves the lower bound and the unique first reversal without floating-point arithmetic.
scientific_limitations: The theorem is restricted to positive-integer vote or seat profiles compared at common total, common actual party count, and common leading-party count. It is an exact finite-resolution ordering result; it neither estimates empirical reversal frequency nor declares one effective-number measure substantively superior.
title: Ten common vote units are the sharp fixed-leader Laakso–Taagepera–Golosov ranking boundary
